rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated threat is emphatic, and thumma marks its greater force; the vision is direct witnessing, the highest certainty, with ʿayn meaning the very essence.
rows.anchor: تكرير للتأكيد وثم للدلالة على الابلغية وجوز أن تكون الرؤية الاولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reports readings of the two visions as seeing the Fire first from afar and then entering it, or as first knowing and then witnessing it; repeated seeing could suggest eternal punishment, though he calls that unlikely.
rows.anchor: وهذا نحو التثنية في قوله تعالى فارجع البصر كرتين وهو خلاف الظاهر جدا

rows.speaker: السيد السند
rows.claim: He defines certainty linguistically as knowledge without doubt and technically as a true, matching belief that something cannot be otherwise and cannot be removed.
rows.anchor: واليقين في اللغة على ما قال السيد السند العلم الذي لاشك فيه وفي الاصطلاح

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: The Raghib ranks certainty above maʿrifa and diraya: it is settled confidence with firm understanding, said of knowledge but not of maʿrifa.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب اليقين من صفة العلم فوق المعرفة والدراية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufi definitions build on technical usage: knowledge by proof is ʿilm al-yaqin, direct unveiling is ʿayn al-yaqin, and tasting the reality is ḥaqq al-yaqin; he illustrates these with death.
rows.anchor: وعلم اليقين بما أعطاه الدليل من ادراك الشىء على ماهو عليه وعين اليقين بما أعطاه المشاهدة والكشف

rows.speaker: ابن عامر والكسائى
rows.claim: They read the first verb with a passive-prefix vowel, while the verse also has variant vowel patterns for the two forms of seeing.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر والكسائى لترون 0 بضم التاء

rows.speaker: علي كرم الله وجهه وابن كثير في رواية وعاصم
rows.claim: They read the first form with fatḥa and the second with ḍamma; Mujahid, Ashhab, and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read both with ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرأعلي كرم الله وجهه وابن كثير في رواية وعاصم كذلك بفتحها في لترون وضمها في لترونها

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبي عمر
rows.claim: They are reported, with disagreement about the attribution, to hamza the two wāws to lighten the heavy ḍamma; the author notes the ḍamma is technically incidental but became fixed in the word.
rows.anchor: وروى عن الحسن وأبي عمر وبخلاف عنهما أنهما همزا الواوين ووجه بانهم استثقلوا الضمة على الواو

rows.speaker: الحسن ومقاتل
rows.claim: They are cited for restricting the address to disbelievers; al-Taybi chooses this view, and Ibn ʿAbbas explicitly identifies the earlier vision-address as polytheists.
rows.anchor: قيل الخطاب للكفار وحكى ذلك عن الحسن ومقاتل واختاره الطيبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, blessing means every pleasure and the question is a rebuke for enjoying blessings without faith; it may come after seeing or entering Hell, when confession is more painful, or at the reckoning before entry.
rows.anchor: وحملوا السؤال هنا على سؤال التقريع والتوبيخ لما أنهم لم يشركوا ذلك بالايمان به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view addresses anyone distracted from religion by worldly life and asks about whatever distracted them; it includes disbelievers and sinful believers and treats the question as reproach.
rows.anchor: وقيل الخطاب مخصوص بكل من ألهاه دنياه عن دينه والنعيم مخصوص بما شغله عن ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view makes the address and question universal but the blessing in question particular; reports then differ over which blessing it is.
rows.anchor: وقيل الخطاب عام وكذا السؤال يعم سؤال التوبيخ وغيره والنعيم خاص

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A raised report identifies the blessing as security and health.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود مرفوعا هو الامن والصحة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali is reported to identify the blessing as well-being.
rows.anchor: عن الامير علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه قال النعيم العافية

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: A raised report from Abu al-Darda names wheat bread, sleeping in shade, and drinking cooled Euphrates water.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الدرداء مرفوعا أكل خبز البر والنوم في الظل وشرب ماء الفرات مبردا

rows.speaker: ثابت البناني
rows.claim: A raised report from Thabit al-Bunani says the blessing is a mouthful of bread, water to quench thirst, and clothing to cover oneself.
rows.anchor: عن ثابت البناني مرفوعا النعيم المسئول عنه يوم القيامة كسرة تقوته وماء يرويه وثوب يواريه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through al-Khatib says the Prophet interpreted the blessing with water and a morsel of bread.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يفسره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وجابر
rows.claim: They are reported to define the blessing as the pleasures of food and drink.
rows.anchor: وروى عنه وعن جابر أنه ملاذ المأكول والمشروب

rows.speaker: الحسين بن فضل
rows.claim: He interprets the blessing as the easing of religious laws and facilitation of the Qurʾan.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسين بن فضل هو تخفيف الشرائع وتيسير القرآن

rows.speaker: جابر الجعفي
rows.claim: In a report to al-Baqir, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq identifies the blessing as the Messenger, through whom God saved the world from error; the account invokes God’s favor in sending a messenger.
rows.anchor: النعيم هو رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم أنعم الله تعالى به على أهل العالم فاستنقذهم به من الضلالة

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: In the report to Abu Hanifa, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq argues that ordinary food and water cannot be the intended reproach; the blessing is the Prophet’s household, through whom people were united and guided to Islam.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو حنيفة فما النعيم قال نحن أهل البيت النعيم أنعم الله تعالى بنا على العباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He judges both reports identifying the blessing with the Prophet or his household unsound, finding signs within the accounts that undermine their authenticity.
rows.anchor: وكلا الخبرين لاأرى لهما صحة وفيهما ما ينادي عن عدم صحتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers a universal address and all blessings; believers are questioned without reproach, while disbelievers are reproached, as a report from Ibn Masʿud states.
rows.anchor: والحق عموم الخطاب والنعيم بيد أن المؤمن لايثرب عليه في شيء ناله منه في الدنيا

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet, Abu Bakr, and ʿUmar went out hungry, were hosted by an Ansari with meat, dates, and drink, then the Prophet said they would be questioned about that blessing.
rows.anchor: بكر وعمرو الذي نفسي بيده لتسئلن عن هذا النعيم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet and companions ate at Abu Ayyub’s home; the Prophet sent food to Fatima and called the bread, meat, and dates blessings for which they would be asked.
rows.anchor: خبز ولحم وتمر وبسر ورطب ودمعت عيناه عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The food in these reports illustrates blessings available at that moment of hunger; it does not restrict the verse, as the wording “some of” confirms.
rows.anchor: وليس المراد في هذا الخبر حصر النعيم مطلقا فيما ذكر بل حصر النعيم بالنسبة إلى ذلك الوقت

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: The universal question covers every blessing, necessary or not, because all gifts must be used in obedience; a report says everyone is asked about life, youth, wealth, and knowledge.
rows.anchor: الحق الكبير الحق أن السؤال يعم المؤمن والكافر عن جميع النعم سواء كان ما لابد منه أولا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A report exempts shade, bread sufficient for strength, and clothing that covers nakedness from accounting.
rows.anchor: ثلاث لايحاسب بهن العبد ظل خص يستظل به وكسرة يشد بها صلبه وثوب يواري به عورته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the exemption report is sound, it means those items escape close scrutiny, or refers to what a person needs for survival; he also doubts a report exempting food eaten with an orphan because it comforts the child and counts as gratitude.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بانه ان اصح فالمراد لايناقش الحساب بهن وقيل المراد مايضطر العبد اليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن الزبير والجمهور
rows.claim: They classify Surat al-ʿAsr as Meccan; Mujahid, Qatada, and Muqatil are cited for classifying it as Medinan, and its three verses are undisputed.
rows.anchor: مكية في قول ابن عباس وابن الزبير والجمهور ومدنية في قول مجاهد وقتادة ومقاتل

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi is reported to say that even if no other surah had been revealed, this one would suffice because it contains the Qurʾan’s sciences.
rows.anchor: انه قال لو لم ينزل غير هذه السورة لكفت الناس لانها شملت جميع علوم القرآن

rows.speaker: أبو حذيفة
rows.claim: He reports that two Companions would recite Surat al-ʿAsr to one another whenever they met, parting only after one recited it and the other greeted him.
rows.anchor: كان الرجلان من اصحاب رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم اذا التقيا لم يفترقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah follows al-Takathur because it points to those whom worldly rivalry did not distract.
rows.anchor: وفيها اشارة إلى حال من لم يلهه التكاثر ولذا وضعت بعد سورته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamz means breaking and lamz stabbing; figuratively they became conventional terms for belittling people, backbiting, and attacking them. The pattern faʿla signals a habitual offender.
rows.anchor: والهمز الكسر كالهزم واللمز الطعن كاللهز شاعا في الكسر من اعراض الناس

rows.speaker: زياد الاعجم
rows.claim: His verse uses hamz and lamz for the person who smiles face-to-face but slanders and mocks when absent.
rows.anchor: اذا لقيتك عن شخط تكاشرني وان تغيبت كنت الهامز اللمزة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies the person as a gossip who divides groups and incites hostility between brothers.
rows.anchor: هو المشاء بالنميمة المفرق بين الجمع المغري بين الاخوان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid distinguishes hamz as attacking people and lamz as attacking their lineages.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد الهمزة الطعان في الناس واللمزة الطعان في الانساب

rows.speaker: أبي العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-ʿAliya says hamz is done to a person’s face and lamz behind their back.
rows.anchor: عن أبي العالية الهمز في الوجه واللمز في الخلف

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj assigns hamz to eye, mouth, and hand gestures, and lamz to the tongue.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج الهمز بالعين والشدق واليد واللمز باللسان

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir reads both medial mims as still; this passive-like pattern denotes someone made a laughingstock, insulted, and mocked.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقر رضى الله تعلى عنه لكل همزة لمزة بسكون الميم فيهما

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Reports connect the revelation with Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Abu ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafi, al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, Umayya ibn Khalaf, Jamil ibn ʿAmir, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, or al-ʿAs ibn Waʾil; it may include them all.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون نازلا في جميع من ذكر لكن استشكل نزولها في الاخنس

rows.speaker: ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar’s sounder biographical account says al-Akhnas became Muslim, creating a problem for assigning him the warning; either that report or his conversion must be unsound.
rows.anchor: على ماصححه ابن حجر في الاصابة أسلم وكان من المؤلفة قلوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the argument that criticizing the unbeliever for mockery is odd because disbelief is worse: losing correct belief is worse than every other evil.
rows.anchor: لان فوت الإعتقاد الصحيح أقبح من كل شيء قبيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla may rebuke the false assumption, hoarding, or mockery; he prefers that it rebuke every blameworthy trait just described. An oath is implicit: their deeds will cast them into the Fire.
rows.anchor: وأنا لاأرى بأسا في كون ذلك ردعا له عن كل ماتضمنته الجمل السابقة من الصفات القبيحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hutama is a fire whose nature is to crush whoever enters it; the intensive pattern presents crushing as habitual, and the root extends to extreme breaking.
rows.anchor: في النار التي من شأنها أن تحطم كل من يلقى فيها وبناء فعلة لتنزيل الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry illustrates hutam for smashing, and Arabic also calls a voracious eater ḥuṭama by comparison with a fire or oven.
rows.anchor: والحطم كسر الشىء كالهشم ثم استعمل لكل كسر متناه

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak interprets al-Hutama as Hell’s fourth level.
rows.anchor: وفسر الضحاك الحطمة هنا بالدرك الرابع من النار

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi calls it Hell’s sixth level, though al-Qushayri transmits from him that it is the second.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي هي الطبقة السادسة من جهنم وحكى القشيرى عنه انها الدرك الثاني

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says al-Hutama is a gate of Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال الواحدي هي باب من أبواب جهنم

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih claims it is the fire in their graves; the author dismisses this interpretation.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو صالح انها النار التي في قبورهم وليس بشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question magnifies al-Hutama by declaring it beyond the grasp of human minds.
rows.anchor: لتهويل أمرها ببيان انها ليست من الامور التي تنالها عقول الخلق

rows.speaker: علي والحسن وابن محيصن وحميد وهرون عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: They read the threat with a dual pronoun referring to the mocker and his wealth; al-Hasan also has a plural reading with the pronoun omitted, referring to every mocker or to him and his followers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي كرم الله وجهه والحسن بخلاف عنه وابن محيصن وحميد وهرون عن أبي عمرو ولينبذان

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr also has a reading with the majestic plural nūn, object pronoun, and emphatic nūn.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي عمرو لننبذنه بنون العظمة وهاء النصب ونو التأكيد

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAli reads al-Hatima with an extra alif after the ḥāʾ.
rows.anchor: وفقرأ زيد بن علي رضى اله تعالى عنه في الحاطمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Nar Allah” is the predicate of an omitted subject, clarifying the Fire’s nature; its attribution to God and description as kindled signal unsurpassed intensity.
rows.anchor: خبر مبتدا محذوف والجملة لبيان شان المسؤل عنها أي نار الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fire rises over and envelops the heart’s center: the heart is the body’s most delicate and sensitive part, and the seat of corrupt beliefs, intentions, dispositions, and deeds.
rows.anchor: تعلوا أوساط القلوب وتغشاها وتخصيصها بالذكر لما أن الفؤاد الطف مافي الجسد

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says the Fire consumes the body until it reaches the heart, then the person is created anew.
rows.anchor: عن محمد بن كعب انه قال في الآية تاكل كل شىء منه حتى تنتهي إلى فؤاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible metaphor is that the Fire perceives the hearts, the source of sins, and punishes each person according to the disposition that warrants their torment.
rows.anchor: فتعلم مافيها فتجازي كلا بحسب مافيه من الصفة المقتضية للعذاب

rows.speaker: ارباب الاشارة
rows.claim: The allegorical interpreters take the verse as pointing to spiritual punishment, which is more severe.
rows.anchor: وارباب الاشارة يقولون ان ما ذكر اشارة إلى العذاب الروحاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muʾṣada means sealed or covered over; fuller discussion is given under Surat al-Balad.
rows.anchor: أي مطبقة وتمام الكلام مر في سورة البلد

rows.speaker: الراغب والفراء
rows.claim: Raghib and al-Farraʾ treat ʿumud as the plural of ʿamud; Abu ʿUbayda instead calls it the plural of ʿimad.
rows.anchor: جمع عمود كما قال الراغب والفراء وقال أبو عبيدة جمع عماد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means tall columns; it can describe the people as bound in stocks with holes for prisoners’ legs, or serve as the predicate of an omitted clause.
rows.anchor: أي طوال والجار والمجرور في موضع الحال من الضمير المجرور في عليهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd is cited for columns made of iron.
rows.anchor: وهي والعياذ بالله تعالى على ماروى عن ابن زيد عمد من حديد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas is cited for columns made of fire; another interpretation has them stretched over sealed doors to make escape hopeless.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير وغيره عن ابن عباس انها من نار واستظهر بعضهم ان العمد تمدد على الابواب

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A long raised report says that after the last believers leave Hell, fiery plates, nails, and columns seal the remaining inhabitants in without openings; they groan forever, explaining the verse.
rows.anchor: فيطبق عليهم بتلك الاطباق ويشد بتلك المسامير وتمدد تلك العمد

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: He treats “in extended columns” as an adjective modifying “sealed”; another permits it as a complement, meaning the doors were shut by the columns, supported by Ibn ʿAbbas’s report about chains across the doors.
rows.anchor: وفي الارشاد عن أبي البقاء انه صفة لمؤصدة وقال بعض لامانع عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine columns can suggest everlasting, intensified punishment for disbelievers who mocked the Prophet; alternatively, prisoner stocks fit the broader class because a backbiter steals people’s reputations like a thief.
rows.anchor: يناسب كون المحدث عنهم كفارا همزوا ولمزوا خير البشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah’s images correspond: mockery crushes reputations, the throw conveys contempt, hoarding stems from the heart and leads to sealing wealth away, and extended columns echo long hopes.
rows.anchor: فانه لما بولغ في الوصف في قوله تعالى همزة لمزة قيل الحطمة للتعادل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan surah has five verses; it follows al-Humaza because the Elephant story shows the worldly destruction of hostile plotters, God’s care for the Prophet, and that wealth cannot avert God’s threat.
rows.anchor: كانه لما تضمن الهمز واللمز من الكفرة نوع كيد له عليه الصلاة والسلام عقب ذلك بقصة أصحاب الفيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to the Prophet; “did you see?” is visual or figurative for knowing, with the cognitive reading more emphatic. Asking how God acted magnifies the astonishing event and displays power, knowledge, wisdom, and the Prophet’s honor.
rows.anchor: الظاهر ان الخطاب لرسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم والهمزة لتقرير رؤيته

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Some allow “how” to be governed by “see” once its interrogative force fades; Abu Hayyan rejects this because it retains interrogative precedence.
rows.anchor: وصرح أبو حيان بامتناعه لانه يراعى صدارته ابقاء لحكم اصله

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن المنذر
rows.claim: Ibrahim ibn al-Mundhir says scholars have no doubt the event occurred in the Prophet’s birth year, making it an early prophetic sign; other chronologies put it ten to seventy years earlier.
rows.anchor: شيخ البخاري لايشك في ذلك أحد من العلماء وعليه الاجماع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas is cited as saying the Prophet was born on the Year of the Elephant; the Suhayli’s favored account instead places his birth fifty days after the event.
rows.anchor: وهو ظاهر قول ابن عباس ولد عليه الصلاة والسلام يوم الفيل وذهب السهيلي أنه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم ولد بعدها بخمسين يوما

rows.speaker: الدمياطي
rows.claim: Al-Dimyati gives fifty-five days between the event and birth; other accounts say forty days or one month.
rows.anchor: وقال الحافظ الدمياطي بخمسة وخمسن يوما وقيل باربعين وقيل بشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “your Lord” hints at the event as a prophetic sign; its protection of the House and Abraham’s prayer do not exclude that purpose, since causes can multiply.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله تعالى ربك نوع رمز إلى الارهاص وكون ذلك لشرف البيت ودعوة الخليل عليه السلام لاينافي الارهاص

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq and others identify Abraha as the Abyssinian ruler called Abu Yaksum; the epithet al-Ashram came from Arbat’s blow that split his brow, nose, eye, and lip.
rows.anchor: وهو الذي يكنى بأبي يكسوم بالسين المهملة ولايأباه التسمية بابرهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After defeating Arbat and taking Yemen’s rule, Abraha built the grand al-Qullays church in Sanaʿa and vowed to redirect Arab pilgrimage from Mecca to it.
rows.anchor: ثم أنه بنى بصنعاء كنيسة لم يرى مثلها في زمانها القليس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An angry man from Kinana desecrated the church after hearing Abraha’s vow; another account says a wind carried a fire lit by Arab travelers and burned it.
rows.anchor: غضب رجل من النساءة أحد بني فقيم ابن عدي من كنانة فخرج حتى أتاها فقعد فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The desecration provoked Abraha to swear that he would march on Mecca and demolish the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: فاستشاط أبرهة غضبا وحلف ليسيرن إلى البيت حتى يهدمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha’s force is variously said to number sixty thousand, with Mahmud and twelve or eight other elephants, a thousand elephants, or only Mahmud; the last is most common and best fits the verse’s apparent wording.
rows.anchor: وقيل معه محمود فقط وهوقول الاكثرين الاوفق بظاهر الآية

rows.speaker: ذو نفر ونفيل ابن حبيب
rows.claim: Dhu Nafar and then Nufayl ibn Habib rallied Yemenis and other Arabs against Abraha, but were defeated and captured; each secured release by arguing his life might be useful.
rows.anchor: خرج اليه رجل من اشراف اليمن وملوكهم يقال له ذو نفر بمن أطاعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraha adorned al-Qullays with colored marble and stones decorated in gold, reportedly taken from Queen Bilqis’s palace.
rows.anchor: وكان ينقل اليها الرخام المجزع والحجارة المنقوشة بالذهب

rows.speaker: صاحب القاموس
rows.claim: The Qamus author prefers that the grave belonged to a different Abu Righal, a Thamudite who left the sanctuary and suffered his people’s punishment, citing a report from Ibn ʿUmar; al-Jawhari had objected to two men sharing the name.
rows.anchor: واختاره صاحب القاموس ذاكرا فيه حديثا رواه أبو دواد في سننه وغيره عن ابن عمر مرفوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Abraha saw ʿAbd al-Muttalib, he found him among the most handsome and distinguished people and treated him with respect.
rows.anchor: وكان عبد المطلب أوسم الناس وأجملهم فلما رآه أكرمه

rows.speaker: عبد المطلب
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Muttalib tells the envoy that Quraysh will not fight because they lack the power, while the sanctuary belongs to God and Abraham, who may protect it or leave Abraha to it.
rows.anchor: هذا بيت الله الحرام وبيت خليله إبراهيم عليه السلام فان يمنعه منه فهو بيته وحرمه

rows.speaker: ذو نفر
rows.claim: Though captive, Dhu Nafar arranges for the elephant keeper Unays to introduce ʿAbd al-Muttalib to Abraha and advocate for him.
rows.anchor: الا ان أنيسا سائس اليل سارسل ايه فأوصيه بك وأعظم عليه حقك

rows.speaker: أبرهة
rows.claim: Abraha receives ʿAbd al-Muttalib respectfully but is disappointed when he asks only for his camels, accusing him of valuing livestock above the House he came to destroy.
rows.anchor: قد كنت أعجبني حين رأيتك ثم قد زهدت فيك حين كلمتني في مائتي بعير

rows.speaker: عبد المطلب
rows.claim: He answers that he owns the camels while the House has its own Lord to protect it; Abraha says God cannot prevent him, and ʿAbd al-Muttalib leaves the outcome to him.
rows.anchor: اني رب الابل وان للبت ربا سيمنعه قال ماكن ليمنع مني قال أنت وذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account has leaders of Bakr and Hudhayl offer Abraha a third of Tihama’s wealth to turn back, but he refuses; Quraysh then shelter in mountain ravines.
rows.anchor: فعرضا عليه ثلث أموال أهل تهامة على أن يرجع ولا يهدم البيت فأبى

rows.speaker: عبد المطلب
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Muttalib holds the Kaaba’s ring with Quraysh, praying and seeking God’s help against the army.
rows.anchor: ثم قال فأخذ بحلقة باب الكعبة ومعه نفر من قريش يدعون الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: نفيل بن حبيب
rows.claim: Nufayl tells Mahmud the elephant to kneel and return from the sacred land; the elephant refuses to face Mecca, though it moves toward Yemen or Syria. One account assigns the command to ʿAbd al-Muttalib.
rows.anchor: فأخذ باذنه فقال ابرك محمود وارجع راشدا من حيث جئت فانك في بلد الله الحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The birds are said to be dark, green, or white like swallows, each carrying three lethal stones; they strike heads, exit below, and cause flesh to fall away.
rows.anchor: وأرسل الله تعالى طيرا من البحر قيل سودا وقيل خضرا وقيل بيضا مثل الخطاطيف

rows.speaker: نفيل
rows.claim: Seeing the army’s defeat, Nufayl recites that Abraha has lost and the people flee, asking where they can escape from the pursuing God.
rows.anchor: أين المفر والاله الطالب والاشرم المغلوب ليس الغالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The army scattered and died along the roads; Abraha’s body deteriorated piece by piece until he reached Sanaʿa barely alive and his chest split open.
rows.anchor: وأصيب أبرهة في جسده وخرجوا به معهم تسقط انملة انملة

rows.speaker: ابن الزبعري
rows.claim: The author refers readers to Ibn al-Zibaʿra’s poem about Mecca and the Elephant episode.
rows.anchor: وقد أشار إلى ذلك ابن الزبعري بقوله من أبيات يذكر فيها مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accounts disagree whether all the army died, whether one survivor reached the Negus before a bird killed him, and whether the elephant’s driver and keeper survived blind and paralyzed; ʿAisha is cited for the last claim.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضهم انه لم ينج منهم غير واحد دخل على النجاشي فاخبره الخبر

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says those struck developed lesions; a report from Yaʿqub ibn ʿUtba calls that year the first appearance of measles and smallpox among Arabs and mentions newly seen wild plants.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة انه من أصابه الحجر جدرته وهو في أول جدري ظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A scouting son returns to say the force was crushed; ʿAbd al-Muttalib then takes the abandoned property and thanks God for restraining the Abyssinians and elephants.
rows.anchor: فلما رأى ذلك أبوه قال ألا ان ابني أفرس العرب

rows.speaker: السلمي
rows.claim: Al-Sulami reads “alam tara” with a very short, still raʾ, to make the jussive effect audible; proposed explanations of speed or prompt perception are criticized because shortening signals less seeing, not shorter time.
rows.anchor: وقرأ السلمي ألم تر بسكون الراء جدا في اظهار أثر الجازم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question summarizes how God nullified the plot to destroy the Kaaba and strip its people of honor; “misguiding” derives from becoming lost and here means rendering their plan void.
rows.anchor: كأنه قبل قد جعل كيدهم في تعطيل الكعبة وتخريبها وصرف شرف أهلها لهم في تضييع وابطال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays was called al-Dalil because he lost and squandered his father’s kingdom.
rows.anchor: ومنه قيل لامرىء القيس الضليل لانه ضلل ملك أبيه وضيعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ababil means successive groups; proposed singulars include ibala, a bundle of firewood, or forms such as ubul and abil, while Abu ʿUbayda and al-Farraʾ say it has no singular of the same form.
rows.anchor: أي جماعات أي جمع ابالة بكسر الهمزة وتشديد الباء الموحدة

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited line about the earth and traveling horses uses ababil for scattered groups; it supports the plural sense.
rows.anchor: اذ الأرض بالجرد الابابيل وقيل واحده ابول مثل عجول وعقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports place the birds’ origin by the sea and say they were neither Najdi, Tihami, nor Hijazi; claims that sanctuary pigeons descend from them or that they nest between earth and sky are unsound.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعض ان حمام الحرم من نسلها ولايصح ذلك

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima describes the birds as having faces like predatory beasts, unlike anything seen before or afterward.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة كأن وجوهوها مثل وجوه اسباع لم تر قبل ذلك ولابعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present-tense “they pelt” vividly reenacts the event; the alternative masculine reading refers to the birds, treated as a masculine collective, though some allow either gender.
rows.anchor: صفة أخرى لطير وعبر بالمضارع لحكاية الحال واستحضار تلك الصورة البديعة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan allows both masculine and feminine agreement for the collective noun; the suggestion that the pronoun refers to God is judged weak.
rows.anchor: وقيل يجوز الامران وهو ظاهر كلام أبى حيان وقيل الضمير عائد على ربك وليس بذاك

rows.speaker: صاحب النشر
rows.claim: Al-Nashr’s author says Abu Hanifa had no recitation and that readings attributed to him are fabricated.
rows.anchor: وعن صاحب النشر أنه رضى الله تعالى عنه لاقراءة له وان القراآت المنسوبة له موضوعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sijjil may be Persian sang-gil, stone and clay; Arabic alternatives derive it from a large bucket pouring many stones, from sending, or from the written register of punishment.
rows.anchor: أي كائنة من طين متحجر معرب سنك كل وقيل هو عربى من السجل بالكسر

rows.speaker: نوفل بن أبى معاوية الديلمى
rows.claim: Nawfal ibn Abi Muʿawiya says he saw the stones: about chickpea size, larger than lentils, reddish and like agate from Zafar.
rows.anchor: انه قال رأيت الحصى التى رمى بها اصحاب الفيل حصى مثل الحمص واكبر من العدس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Reports from Ibn ʿAbbas give the stones as hazelnut-sized in one account and sheep droppings in another.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال حجارة مثل البندق وفى رواية ابن مردويه عنه مثل بعر الغنم

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr describes birds from the sea’s south side carrying large camel-like stones, with the smallest head-sized, and says whoever was struck died.
rows.anchor: عن عبيد بن عمير أنه قال فى الآية هى طير خرجت من قبلة البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relied-upon account has birds about the size of swallows and stones ranging around chickpea size; Abu Salih’s report says a victim’s and father’s names were written on each stone.
rows.anchor: والمعول عليه ان الطير فى الحجم كالخطاطيف وأن الحجارة منها ماهو كالحمصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eaten chaff may be crop leaves eaten by worms or stripped of their grain; the image signifies bodies without spirits or burned insides. Another view compares their dismembered bodies to scattered dung, with Qurʾanic decorum avoiding that word; a further view makes them discarded, unprotected straw.
rows.anchor: كورق زرع وقع فيه الاكال وهو أن يأكله الدود أوأكل حبه فبقى صفرا منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their destruction by stones suits their attempt to destroy the Kaaba; other proposed links are the Kinani’s excrement that provoked Abraha, or fire carried by wind that burned the church.
rows.anchor: وكأنه لما أن مجيئهم لهدم الكعبة ناسب اهلاكهم بالحجارة

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Abu al-Darda is reported to read maʾkul with fatḥa on the hamza, by vowel assimilation; the author calls the reading anomalous and compares maḥmum.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو الدرداء فيما نقل ابن خالويه ماكول بفتح الهمزة اتباعا لحركة الميم

rows.speaker: الضحاك وابن السائب
rows.claim: The introduction calls Surat Quraysh, also Surat Li-ilaf Quraysh; most classify it as Meccan, while al-Dahhak and Ibn al-Saʾib call it Medinan. Verse counts differ by regional tradition.
rows.anchor: مكية في قول الجمهور مدنية في قول الضحاك وابن السائب

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Those who regard al-Fil and Quraysh as one surah cite Ubayy’s codex without a basmala between them and ʿUmar’s Maghrib recitation of both without a pause.
rows.anchor: ان أبي بن كعب لم يفصل بينهما في مصحفه بالبسملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author answers that some codices do mark the separation, and the report may reflect inaudible recitation or a recitation he did not hear; an Umm Hani report and other evidence supports an independent surah, while tawatur makes extra proof unnecessary.
rows.anchor: وانت تعلم انه بعد ثبوت تواثر الفصل لايحتاج إلى شيء مما يذكر

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafaji derives ilaf as a verbal noun from either alifa or alafa; al-Raghib glosses it as harmonious joining, while al-Harawi says it means treaties between Quraysh and foreign rulers. Alusi notes treaty is not the majority view.
rows.anchor: الايلاف على ماقال الخفاجي مصدر ألفت الشيء وآلفته

rows.speaker: الهروي
rows.claim: Al-Harawi says Hashim contracted with Syria’s ruler and al-Muttalib with the Persian king, while ʿAbd Shams and Nawfal made agreements with Egypt and Abyssinia.
rows.anchor: فكان هاشم يؤلف ملك الشام وامطلب كسرى وعبد شمس ونوفل يؤالفان ملك مصر والحبشة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term may derive from the triliteral alifa or the causative alafa, with different verbal-noun forms; a line about a tame gazelle illustrates the transitive causative usage.
rows.anchor: وقد يأتي آلف متعديا لواحد كالف ومنه قوله من المؤلفات الرمل أدماء حرة

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi favors Quraysh as descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinana, supported by the report that the Prophet defined Quraysh as Nadr’s descendants; alternative lineages are disputed.
rows.anchor: وهوأصح الاقوال وأثبتها عند القرطبي قيل وعليه الفقهاء

rows.speaker: الزبير بن بكار
rows.claim: Zubayr ibn Bakkar says genealogists agree Quraysh descend from Fahr; Fahr was also called Quraysh, and Qusay gathered the clans in the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: أجمع النسابون من قريش وغبيرهم على ان قريشا انما تفرقت عن فهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He calls descent from Mukhlad ibn al-Nadr weak and treats claims of descent from Qusay or ʿUrwa as a Rafidite attempt to deny the first two caliphs’ rightful succession.
rows.anchor: وأضعف من ذلك بل هو قول رافضي يريد به نفي حقية خلافة الشيخين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Asked by Muʿawiya why Quraysh had that name, Ibn ʿAbbas compared them to the qirsh, the sea’s strongest creature that eats without being eaten and dominates others.
rows.anchor: وبذلك أجاب ابن عباس معاوية لما ساله لم سميت قريش قريشا

rows.speaker: تبع
rows.claim: Tubbaʿ’s quoted poem likens Quraysh to a fish that eats everything and is unmatched; it continues with a prophecy of a coming prophet and hardship for Quraysh.
rows.anchor: تاكل الغث والسمين ولاتترك يوما لذي جناحين ريشا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ derives Quraysh from taqarrush, meaning earning through trade.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء هو من التقرش بمعنى التكسب سموا بذلك تجارتهم

rows.speaker: الحارث بن حلزة
rows.claim: His line “al-muqarrish” supports deriving the name from probing or searching; Quraysh sought out people with needs in order to help them.
rows.anchor: وقيل من التقريش وهو التفتيش ومنه قول الحرث ابن حلزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another derivation is from gathering: Quraysh reunited after dispersion. The diminutive is either truncation of a derived form or regular for a basic triliteral, and in either case conveys honor.
rows.anchor: وقبل من التقرش وهو من التجمع ومنه قوله اخوة قرشوا الذنوب علينا

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: The nisba may be Qurashi or Qurayshi; the name is declinable when it denotes the community, while making it a tribe-name also permits diptote declension.
rows.anchor: وعن سيبويه أنه قال في نحو معد وقريش وثقيف هذه للاحياء اكثر

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil attaches the causal lām to “so let them worship”; the fa implies a condition: if Quraysh do not worship for all God’s favors, let them worship for this great one.
rows.anchor: واللام في لايلاف للتعليل والجار والمجرور متعلق عند الخليل بقوله فليعبدوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their ilaf” replaces the first ilaf; journey is the object if ilaf means familiarity, but with the treaty sense it has a preposition understood. The specific replacement magnifies the journeys.
rows.anchor: بدل من ايلاف قريش ورحلة مفعول به لايلافهم على تقدير ان يكون من الالفة

rows.speaker: الاخفش والكسائي والفراء
rows.claim: They attach the lām to an implied act such as “marvel,” urging wonder that Quraysh travel yet neglect the God who protected and provided for them, hence the following command to worship.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي والفراء كذلك الا انهما قدرا الفعل بدلالة السياق اعجبوا

rows.speaker: الاخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash also connects the lām to God making the army like eaten chaff; destruction either preserved their trade-security or deterred later attackers, and more than one cause may apply.
rows.anchor: أهلك سبحانه من قصدهم من الحبشة ولم يسلطهم عليهم ليبقوا على ماكانوا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some treat the lām as consequential. Ibn ʿAbbas says Quraysh traveled to Yemen in winter and Busra in summer under the protection of being guardians of God’s sanctuary.
rows.anchor: وقال غير واحد ان اللام للعاقبة وكان لقريش رحتان رحلة في الشتاء إلى اليمن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbas says summer journeys went to Taif for water and shade, and winter journeys to Mecca for trade and other needs.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا أنهم كانوا يرحلون في الصيف إلى الطائف حيث الماء والظل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A singular “journey” can refer to both winter and summer trips when context removes ambiguity; poetic and Qurʾanic examples support singular with a dual referent, against Sibawayh’s restriction to necessity.
rows.anchor: وأفردت الرحلة مع أن المراد رحلتا الشتاء والصيف لأمن اللبس وظهور المعنى

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says Quraysh had four trading journeys; Ibn ʿAtiyya rejects this, while al-Bahr argues four brothers arranged security for Syria, Abyssinia, Yemen, and Persia.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش كانت لهم أربع رحل وتعقبه ابن عطية بأنه قول مردود

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari explains ilaf as a guarantee akin to hired protection; if so, journey can be a collective noun covering four routes, although al-Alusi finds this reading unclear and notes it differs from al-Harawi.
rows.anchor: قال الازهري الايلاف شبه الاجارة بالخفارة فان كان كذلك جاز أن يكون لهم رحل أربع

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmir reads the first phrase without its yāʾ, while the seven readers agree on the yāʾ in “their ilaf”; differing Uthmanic spelling is cited as evidence that readings follow oral transmission.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر لالاف قريش بلا ياء

rows.speaker: أبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: Abu Bakr from ʿAsim is reported to read two hamzas, the second quiescent; this anomalous form drops the first hamza of the root to avoid the heavy sequence.
rows.anchor: فروى عن أبي بكر عن عاصم أنه قرأ بهمزتين فيهما الثانية ساكنة

rows.speaker: محمد بن داود النقار
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Dawud al-Naqqar reports a double-kasra hamza reading followed by a lengthened yāʾ, but the author says he recanted and returned to the majority reading.
rows.anchor: وروى محمد بن داود النقار عن عاصم ائيلافهم بهمزتين مكسورتين

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar is cited for variant forms laʾalf and alifahum; a poetic line contrasts Quraysh’s guaranteed security with others lacking it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر فيما حكى الزمخشري لالف قريش وقرأ فيما حكى ابن عطية الفهم

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وابن عامر
rows.claim: They are also reported to read ilafihim on the faʿal pattern; other Abu Jaʿfar readings use a quiescent yāʾ after the lām by irregular hamza substitution.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي جعفر أيضا وابن عامر الافهم على وزن فعال وعن أبي جعفر أيضا ليلاف بياء ساكنة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima reads layʾalifa in the subjunctive with Quraysh as its subject; he and Hilal ibn Fityan are also cited for opening the lām of the imperative.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة ليألف قريش على صيغة المضارع المنصوب بان مضمرة

rows.speaker: أبو السمال
rows.claim: Abu al-Sammal reads riḥla with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, meaning the destination of travel; with kasra it is a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو السمال رحلة بضم الراء وهي حينئذ بمعنى الجهة التي يرحل اليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This House” means the Kaaba, which God protected from the Elephant army.
rows.anchor: هو الكعبة التي حميت من أصحاب الفيل

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar reportedly pointed at the Kaaba while reciting this verse in prayer there.
rows.anchor: وعن عمر أنه صلى بالناس بمكة عند الكعبة فلما قرأ فليعبدوا رب هذا البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fed Quraysh through their two journeys after severe hunger; another explanation specifies a famine when they ate carrion and bones.
rows.anchor: بسب تينك الرحلتين اللتين تمكنوا منهما بواسطة كونهم من جيرانهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Fear may mean Abraha’s attack, danger from being seized on journeys or at home, or leprosy; Ibn ʿAbbas says God protected them from plague.
rows.anchor: وهو خوف أصحاب الفيل أو خوف من التخطف في بلدهم ومسايرهم أو خوف الجذام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas attributes food to Abraham’s prayer for provision and safety to Abraham’s prayer that the land be secure.
rows.anchor: حيث قال وأرزقهم من الثمرات وآمنهم من خوف حيث قال إبراهيم عليه السلام رب أجعل هذا البلد آمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition min can express cause, with an implied noun or hunger as the motivating cause, or substitution as in “the life of this world instead of the Hereafter.”
rows.anchor: ومن قل تعليلية أي أنعم عليهم وأطعمهم لازالة الجوع عنهم

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani transmits a claim that the caliphate belongs only to Quraysh; the author says this is plainly false.
rows.anchor: وحكى الكرماني في غرائب التفسير انه قيل في قوله تعالى وآمنهم من خوف ان الخلافة لاتكون الا فيهم

rows.speaker: المسيبى عن نافع
rows.claim: Al-Musayyibi from Nafiʿ reads min khawf with the nūn concealed before khāʾ; a similar concealment before ʿayn is also cited.
rows.anchor: وقرأالمسيبى عن نافع من خوف باخفاء النون في الخاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن الزبير والجمهور
rows.claim: The following surah is also called Araʾayta, al-Din, or al-Takdhib; most call it Meccan, while reports give a Medinan setting, and Hibat Allah says half concerns ʿAs ibn Waʾil in Mecca and half ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy in Medina.
rows.anchor: وتسمى سورة أرأيت والدين والتكذيب وهي مكية في قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It has seven verses in the Iraqi count and six elsewhere; its rebuke follows Quraysh’s mention of feeding the hungry, worshiping the Kaaba, and disbelief in resurrection and judgment.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر سبحانه في سورة قريش أطعمهم من جوع ذم عز وجل هنا من لم يحض على طعام المسكين
